           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                        )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                          ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                        )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                         )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                            )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                               )


                          Redacted Confidential Testimony Summary of Gwin Cash

         Direct Testimony

                In his Direct Testimony, Gwin Cash first provided his educational qualifications and
         employment history. He is Senior Manager of Pricing, Rate Administration, and Load Analysis
         for Oklahoma Gas & Electric Company. Mr. Cash testified the purpose of his testimony is to
         explain the various rate design and cost allocation components of the three Electric Service
         Agreements requested for approval in this case, specifically the provisions found in section 5 of
         the ESAs covering applicable tariffs, minimum billing features, cost-of-service study allocator
         treatment, and rate design.

                 Mr. Cash testified that the customer protections contained in the ESAs comport with the
         customer protections described in the Commission’s final order in Case No. PUD 2025-000038.
         He explained that the Commission’s order in that case identified several benefits of a new large
         load tariff, including rates developed from allocations specific to very large load sizes,
         accommodation of unique energy needs and service agreement durations, and the ability to employ
         customer and system protections such as minimum bills, contract lengths, and other requirements.
         He stated that these benefits and certain other customer protections are included in various forms
         in the special contracts requested for approval. He further testified that while the terms and
         conditions of a new large load tariff are not yet known, the ESAs provide that the non-rate terms
         and conditions of the ESAs will control over the terms and conditions of any subsequent tariff, and
         that the new large load tariff, if approved and determined to be applicable to Google, will adjust
         the base rate pricing of the customer, energy, demand, and other charges.

                 Mr. Cash then testified regarding the minimum billing features of the ESAs, explaining
         that they are designed to ensure an appropriate amount of cost recovery by establishing a baseline
         level of charges that apply regardless of actual usage, thereby reducing risk and protecting other
         customers from potential cost shifts. He stated that there are two primary components described
         in section 5.02 of the ESAs: a Minimum Billing Demand Charge and a Minimum Billing Energy
         Charge. He explained that the Minimum Billing Demand Charge is calculated as the product of
         the demand charges, expressed as dollars per kilowatt, and a Minimum Billing Demand set at
         of the ESAs’ Contract Demand, with the billed demand being the greater of this minimum value
         or actual measured demand corrected for power factor. He further explained that the

                 Mr. Cash stated that the billing minimums will have applicability to any tariff that serves
         as a rate recovery mechanism for fixed costs, including the base rate tariff, Large Power and Light
         Time-of-Use, and riders that serve as fixed cost recovery for periods in between general rate case
         proceedings, such as the Generation Capacity Rider, Grid Enhancement Mechanism, and the
         Interim Rate Rider. He added that the allocated portion of capacity costs included for recovery in
         the Fuel Cost Adjustment rider will also be subject to the billing minimums, while all other riders’
         energy and demand charges will be subject to actual metered energy and demand. He testified that
         because these billing minimums are tied to fixed cost recovery tariffs, they ensure an adequate
         level of revenue tied to the capital investments incurred by these ESAs, and that absent a minimum
         amount of revenues from large customers like Google, there could be adverse impacts on other
         customers in their specific customer class and other customer classes.

                 Mr. Cash testified that for the purpose of cost allocation during general rate case
         proceedings, Google’s contract demand will be utilized to allocate costs to Google, ensuring that
         adequate cost is allocated through the LPL-TOU or other applicable rate class. He explained that
         this approach stands in contrast to the common practice of utilizing actual test year demands, which
         would be less than the contract demands and would result in lower cost allocations potentially
         being shifted to other customer classes. He stated that this cost allocation proposal protects against
         any negative allocation to other customer classes. Mr. Cash concluded by recommending that the
         Commission approve the special contracts as filed, inclusive of the rate design, tariff applicability,
         cost allocation, and bill minimum provisions as described in his testimony and found in sections
         5.01(a), 5.02, and 5.03 of the special contracts.
